claim: Maturing oocytes and early embryos lack appreciable transcription.
source: Because maturing oocytes and early embryos lack appreciable transcription, posttranscriptional regulatory processes control their development.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about early development in many organisms.

claim: Posttranscriptional regulatory processes control development of maturing oocytes and early embryos.
source: Because maturing oocytes and early embryos lack appreciable transcription, posttranscriptional regulatory processes control their development.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcription and is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Translational-efficiency changes correspond to tail-length changes until gastrulation in Drosophila.
source: The correspondence between translational-efficiency changes and tail-length changes indicated that tail-length changes broadly regulate translation until gastrulation, when this coupling disappears.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from PAL-seq and ribosome profiling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coupling between translational efficiency and poly(A)-tail length disappears at gastrulation.
source: The correspondence between translational-efficiency changes and tail-length changes indicated that tail-length changes broadly regulate translation until gastrulation, when this coupling disappears.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During egg activation, relative changes in poly(A)-tail length and translational efficiency were largely retained in the absence of cytoplasmic polyadenylation.
source: During egg activation, relative changes in poly(A)-tail length, and thus translational efficiency, were largely retained in the absence of cytoplasmic polyadenylation, which indicated that selective poly(A)-tail shortening primarily specifies these changes.
evidence: This is supported by data from wispy-mutant experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Selective poly(A)-tail shortening primarily specifies changes in translational efficiency during egg activation.
source: During egg activation, relative changes in poly(A)-tail length, and thus translational efficiency, were largely retained in the absence of cytoplasmic polyadenylation, which indicated that selective poly(A)-tail shortening primarily specifies these changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that relative changes are preserved without cytoplasmic polyadenylation.

claim: Many translational changes depend on PAN GU and Smaug.
source: Many translational changes depended on PAN GU and Smaug, and these changes were largely attributable to tail-length changes.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with png and smg mutants shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Translational changes dependent on PAN GU and Smaug are largely attributable to tail-length changes.
source: Many translational changes depended on PAN GU and Smaug, and these changes were largely attributable to tail-length changes.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses between tail-length and TE changes in mutant backgrounds.

claim: Tail-length–independent mechanisms maintain translation despite tail-length shortening during oocyte maturation.
source: Our results also revealed the presence of tail-length–independent mechanisms that maintained translation despite tail-length shortening during oocyte maturation, and prevented essentially all translation of bicoid and several other mRNAs before egg activation.
evidence: This is supported by observations in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing mRNAs that maintain translation despite tail shortening.

claim: Tail-length–independent mechanisms prevent essentially all translation of bicoid mRNA before egg activation.
source: Our results also revealed the presence of tail-length–independent mechanisms that maintained translation despite tail-length shortening during oocyte maturation, and prevented essentially all translation of bicoid and several other mRNAs before egg activation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing bicoid has minimal translation in oocytes despite having poly(A) tails, as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 4.

claim: Spermatogenesis produces haploid sperm capable of penetrating the oocyte.
source: Spermatogenesis produces haploid sperm capable of penetrating the oocyte, whereas oogenesis produces differentiated oocytes that are stockpiled with maternal nutrients, proteins, and mRNAs, and have outer layers that protect the embryo and enable fertilization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gametogenesis.

claim: Oogenesis produces differentiated oocytes that are stockpiled with maternal nutrients, proteins, and mRNAs.
source: Spermatogenesis produces haploid sperm capable of penetrating the oocyte, whereas oogenesis produces differentiated oocytes that are stockpiled with maternal nutrients, proteins, and mRNAs, and have outer layers that protect the embryo and enable fertilization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oogenesis.

claim: In most animals the oocyte is arrested in meiosis.
source: In most animals the oocyte is arrested in meiosis, and fertilization leads to initiation of mitosis as the oocyte nucleus completes meiosis and fuses with the haploid sperm nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte development.

claim: Fertilization leads to initiation of mitosis as the oocyte nucleus completes meiosis and fuses with the haploid sperm nucleus.
source: In most animals the oocyte is arrested in meiosis, and fertilization leads to initiation of mitosis as the oocyte nucleus completes meiosis and fuses with the haploid sperm nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fertilization.

claim: Fertilization leads to changes in mRNA translation and protein stability.
source: Fertilization also leads to changes in mRNA translation and protein stability, which support a period of development driven off of maternal stockpiles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about post-fertilization development.

claim: The initial stage of maternal control lasts for 1–2 mitotic divisions in mammals.
source: After this initial stage of maternal control, which lasts for 1–2 mitotic divisions in mammals and 13 mitotic divisions in Drosophila, widespread transcription begins from the zygotic nuclei (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: The initial stage of maternal control lasts for 13 mitotic divisions in Drosophila.
source: After this initial stage of maternal control, which lasts for 1–2 mitotic divisions in mammals and 13 mitotic divisions in Drosophila, widespread transcription begins from the zygotic nuclei (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: Oocyte maturation involves the release of the primary meiotic arrest at prophase I and progression of the oocyte nucleus into meiotic divisions.
source: Oocyte maturation involves the release of the primary meiotic arrest at prophase I and progression of the oocyte nucleus into meiotic divisions to produce a mature oocyte (egg) capable of being fertilized (Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011.

claim: The mature oocyte is arrested in metaphase II in most vertebrates.
source: The mature oocyte is arrested in metaphase II in most vertebrates and metaphase I in insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte development.

claim: The mature oocyte is arrested in metaphase I in insects.
source: The mature oocyte is arrested in metaphase II in most vertebrates and metaphase I in insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect oocyte development.

claim: Egg activation is coupled to fertilization in most animals.
source: The OET requires egg activation, which is coupled to fertilization in most animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fertilization and egg activation.

claim: Egg activation releases the secondary meiotic arrest, allowing completion of meiosis.
source: Egg activation releases the secondary meiotic arrest, allowing completion of meiosis (Horner and Wolfner, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horner and Wolfner, 2008.

claim: The MZT marks the transfer of control of development from the mother to the zygote as maternal mRNAs are degraded, transcription from the zygotic genome begins, and embryonic development becomes dependent on zygotic gene products.
source: The MZT marks the transfer of control of development from the mother to the zygote as maternal mRNAs are degraded, transcription from the zygotic genome begins, and embryonic development becomes dependent on zygotic gene products (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claim: In Xenopus, zebrafish, and Drosophila the major activation of zygotic transcription occurs as the cell cycle lengthens and gastrulation begins.
source: In Xenopus, zebrafish, and Drosophila the major activation of zygotic transcription occurs as the cell cycle lengthens and gastrulation begins, a developmental period referred to as the midblastula transition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the midblastula transition.

claim: Poly(A)-tail length and TE were correlated in cleavage-stage embryos (0–1 hr embryo).
source: Indeed, poly(A)-tail length and TE were correlated in cleavage-stage embryos (0–1 hr embryo), and the slope of this relationship was steep, such that small differences in poly(A)-tail length corresponded to large differences in TE (Figure 1B; e.g., the median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was >5 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was >5 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt in 0-1 hr embryos.
source: Indeed, poly(A)-tail length and TE were correlated in cleavage-stage embryos (0–1 hr embryo), and the slope of this relationship was steep, such that small differences in poly(A)-tail length corresponded to large differences in TE (Figure 1B; e.g., the median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was >5 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Changes in TE correlated with changes in tail length when progressing through the OET.
source: Likewise, when progressing through the OET, the changes in TE correlated with the changes in tail length (Figure 1B, 0–1 hr embryo / Stage 14 oocyte).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A positive correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE persisted in the 2–3 hr embryos.
source: Although a positive correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE persisted in the 2–3 hr embryos, the slope of this relationship strongly diminished such that the median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was <2 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt, as expected if poly(A)-tail length changes were no longer used to influence translation in these cellularized and gastrulating embryos.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The slope of the relationship between poly(A)-tail length and TE strongly diminished in 2-3 hr embryos such that the median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was <2 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt.
source: Although a positive correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE persisted in the 2–3 hr embryos, the slope of this relationship strongly diminished such that the median TE of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt was <2 fold greater than that of mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt, as expected if poly(A)-tail length changes were no longer used to influence translation in these cellularized and gastrulating embryos.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: The changes in poly(A)-tail length that occurred between cleavage-stage and cellularized embryos were not positively correlated with the changes in TE.
source: Indeed, the changes in poly(A)-tail length that occurred between cleavage-stage and cellularized embryos were not positively correlated with the changes in TE (Figure 1B, 2–3 hr embryo / 0–1 hr embryo).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The positive correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE disappeared in 3–4 hr embryos and 5–6 hr embryos.
source: The positive correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE disappeared in subsequent stages of gastrulation (3–4 hr embryos and 5–6 hr embryos), and although tail lengths changed between these stages, the TE changes spanned a very narrow range (Figure 1B, 3–4 hr embryo / 2–3 hr embryo and 5–6 hr embryo / 3–4 hr embryo).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The TE of zelda mRNA increased markedly during the OET.
source: For example, the TE of mRNAs for zelda and stat92E, two transcription factors required for the onset of zygotic transcription at the MZT (Liang et al., 2008; Harrison and Eisen, 2015), increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), as expected if translational activation of these mRNAs produces the proteins necessary to initiate the MZT, and accounting for the previously noted increase in Zelda protein in early embryos (Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: The TE of stat92E mRNA increased markedly during the OET.
source: For example, the TE of mRNAs for zelda and stat92E, two transcription factors required for the onset of zygotic transcription at the MZT (Liang et al., 2008; Harrison and Eisen, 2015), increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), as expected if translational activation of these mRNAs produces the proteins necessary to initiate the MZT, and accounting for the previously noted increase in Zelda protein in early embryos (Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: Zelda and Stat92E are transcription factors required for the onset of zygotic transcription at the MZT.
source: For example, the TE of mRNAs for zelda and stat92E, two transcription factors required for the onset of zygotic transcription at the MZT (Liang et al., 2008; Harrison and Eisen, 2015), increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), as expected if translational activation of these mRNAs produces the proteins necessary to initiate the MZT, and accounting for the previously noted increase in Zelda protein in early embryos (Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2008 and Harrison and Eisen, 2015.

claim: Zelda protein increases in early embryos.
source: For example, the TE of mRNAs for zelda and stat92E, two transcription factors required for the onset of zygotic transcription at the MZT (Liang et al., 2008; Harrison and Eisen, 2015), increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), as expected if translational activation of these mRNAs produces the proteins necessary to initiate the MZT, and accounting for the previously noted increase in Zelda protein in early embryos (Harrison and Eisen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison and Eisen, 2015.

claim: The TE of smaug mRNA increased markedly during the OET.
source: Likewise, the TE of smaug and bicoid mRNA increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), yielding factors essential for embryonic development and patterning, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The TE of bicoid mRNA increased markedly during the OET.
source: Likewise, the TE of smaug and bicoid mRNA increased markedly during the OET (Figure 1C), yielding factors essential for embryonic development and patterning, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were well correlated at stages 11, 12, and 13 (Rs ≥0.51).
source: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were well correlated at stages 11, 12, and 13 (Rs ≥0.51), but poorly correlated at stage 14 (Rs = 0.20) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were poorly correlated at stage 14 (Rs = 0.20).
source: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were well correlated at stages 11, 12, and 13 (Rs ≥0.51), but poorly correlated at stage 14 (Rs = 0.20) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The c-mos mRNA and several cyclin mRNAs undergo tail-length increases that correspond to translational activation during Xenopus oocyte maturation.
source: Previously, the relationship between poly(A)-tail length and translation had been examined for the c-mos mRNA and several cyclin mRNAs during Xenopus oocyte maturation (Sheets et al., 1994; Barkoff et al., 1998; Piqué et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nearly half (46%) of mRNAs exceeding read cutoffs had net TE changes of ≥2 fold over the course of oocyte maturation.
source: Of the mRNAs exceeding our read cutoffs, nearly half (46%) had net TE changes of ≥2 fold over the course of oocyte maturation, with mRNAs for 1264 and 1037 genes up- or downregulated, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mRNAs for 1264 genes were translationally upregulated during oocyte maturation.
source: Of the mRNAs exceeding our read cutoffs, nearly half (46%) had net TE changes of ≥2 fold over the course of oocyte maturation, with mRNAs for 1264 and 1037 genes up- or downregulated, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: mRNAs for 1037 genes were translationally downregulated during oocyte maturation.
source: Of the mRNAs exceeding our read cutoffs, nearly half (46%) had net TE changes of ≥2 fold over the course of oocyte maturation, with mRNAs for 1264 and 1037 genes up- or downregulated, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: Far fewer mRNAs (1.5%) changed in abundance ≥2 fold during oocyte maturation (25 mRNAs increased, and 52 mRNAs decreased).
source: In contrast, far fewer mRNAs (1.5%) changed in abundance ≥2 fold (25 mRNAs increased, and 52 mRNAs decreased), indicating the posttranscriptional nature of this regulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from RNA-seq data.

claim: The regulation during oocyte maturation is posttranscriptional in nature.
source: In contrast, far fewer mRNAs (1.5%) changed in abundance ≥2 fold (25 mRNAs increased, and 52 mRNAs decreased), indicating the posttranscriptional nature of this regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TE changes greatly exceed mRNA abundance changes.

claim: Cyclin B mRNA is included in the set of mRNAs that showed progressive increases in relative TE at each stage of oogenesis.
source: The relative TEs for some mRNAs increased progressively at each stage of oogenesis (Figure 3A cluster 1), and this set of mRNAs included cyclin B (Figure 3B), whose translational control via polyadenylation is reported to be crucial for oocyte maturation (Benoit et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Translational control of cyclin B via polyadenylation is crucial for oocyte maturation.
source: The relative TEs for some mRNAs increased progressively at each stage of oogenesis (Figure 3A cluster 1), and this set of mRNAs included cyclin B (Figure 3B), whose translational control via polyadenylation is reported to be crucial for oocyte maturation (Benoit et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benoit et al., 2005.

claim: Changes in TE correlated poorly with previously measured changes in protein abundance during oocyte maturation (Rs = 0.15).
source: Moreover, changes in TE correlated poorly with previously measured changes in protein abundance (Kronja et al., 2014a), potentially due to a large role of posttranslational regulation during this time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Rs = 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The net changes in TE and poly(A)-tail length over the course of oocyte maturation were largely concordant for both translationally up- and downregulated mRNAs.
source: The net changes in TE and poly(A)-tail length over the course of oocyte maturation were largely concordant for both translationally up- and downregulated mRNAs, indicating strong coupling between TE and poly(A)-tail length during oocyte maturation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A set of mRNAs underwent substantial tail-length reductions between oocyte stages 13 and 14 without concordant TE reductions.
source: Nonetheless, a potential deviation from the typical coupled behavior occurred between oocyte stages 13 and 14, when a set of mRNAs that underwent substantial tail-length reductions did not undergo concordant TE reductions (Figure 2, Stage 14 / Stage 13, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mRNAs for 22 of the 30 genes encoding subunits of the proteasome underwent substantial tail shortening between stages 13 and 14 but remained well translated.
source: Notable among this set were mRNAs for 22 of the 30 genes encoding subunits of the proteasome (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Between oocyte stages 11 through 14, the TEs of cyclin B, cyclin B3, and fizzy mRNAs increased 103, 248, and 319 fold, respectively.
source: Between oocyte stages 11 through 14, the TEs of these mRNAs increased 103, 248, and 319 fold (compared to a median TE change of only 1.3 fold), respectively, whereas poly(A)-tail lengths increased 1.6, 2.4, and 2.0 fold (compared to the median of 1.2 fold) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Between oocyte stages 11 through 14, the poly(A)-tail lengths of cyclin B, cyclin B3, and fizzy mRNAs increased 1.6, 2.4, and 2.0 fold, respectively.
source: Between oocyte stages 11 through 14, the TEs of these mRNAs increased 103, 248, and 319 fold (compared to a median TE change of only 1.3 fold), respectively, whereas poly(A)-tail lengths increased 1.6, 2.4, and 2.0 fold (compared to the median of 1.2 fold) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mRNAs from 121 genes were very poorly translated in stage 11 oocytes (TE ≤ 0.1) and became ≥10-fold better translated during oocyte maturation.
source: In addition to these examples, mRNAs from 121 other genes were very poorly translated in stage 11 oocytes (TE ≤ 0.1) and became ≥10-fold better translated during oocyte maturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For cyclin B, cyclin B3 and fizzy mRNAs, the distribution of poly(A)-tail lengths remained unimodal as overall lengths increased.
source: However, for cyclin B, cyclin B3 and fizzy mRNAs, the distribution of poly(A)-tail lengths remained unimodal as overall lengths increased, which indicated that the focus on the mean tail-length change in our analyses did not miss specific regulation of a subset of mRNAs for a gene (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: During oocyte maturation, the steepness of the relationship between poly(A)-tail length and TE implied a 6- to 7-fold increase in the median TE for mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt relative to those with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt in stages 11, 12, and 13 oocytes.
source: The steepness of this relationship in stage 11, 12, and 13 oocytes implied a 6- to 7-fold increase in the median TE for mRNAs with a poly(A)-tail length between 70–80 nt relative to those with a poly(A)-tail length between 30–40 nt.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In stage 14 oocytes, the poor correlation between tail length and TE resulted in only a 1.8-fold increase in median TE when comparing mRNAs with poly(A)-tail lengths between 70-80 nt and 30-40 nt.
source: In stage 14 oocytes, the poor correlation between tail length and TE resulted in only a 1.8-fold increase in median TE when comparing mRNAs with such tail lengths.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Egg activation occurs rapidly (within ~20 min).
source: Although egg activation occurs rapidly (within ~20 min) (Horner and Wolfner, 2008), this developmental transition induced TE changes for mRNAs from many genes, some of which exceeded 30 fold (Figure 2, lower right) (Kronja et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horner and Wolfner, 2008.

claim: Egg activation induced TE changes for mRNAs from many genes, some of which exceeded 30 fold.
source: Although egg activation occurs rapidly (within ~20 min) (Horner and Wolfner, 2008), this developmental transition induced TE changes for mRNAs from many genes, some of which exceeded 30 fold (Figure 2, lower right) (Kronja et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citation to Kronja et al., 2014b.

claim: During egg activation the correlation between tail-length change and TE change exceeded that observed for any other transition.
source: Indeed, during egg activation the correlation between tail-length change and TE change exceeded that observed for any other transition (Figure 1B and Figure 2, lower panels; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of correlation coefficients across different developmental transitions shown in Figures 1B, 2, and 4A.

claim: mRNAs for the embryonic patterning genes bicoid, torso, and Toll are translationally upregulated during egg activation in a manner reported to depend on changes in poly(A)-tail length.
source: mRNAs for the embryonic patterning genes bicoid, torso, and Toll are translationally upregulated during egg activation in a manner reported to depend on changes in poly(A)-tail length (Salles et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salles et al., 1994.

claim: Translation of bicoid mRNA was undetectable or detected with very few reads in oocytes from stages 11 through 14.
source: In our analyses, translation of bicoid mRNA was undetectable or detected with very few reads in oocytes from stages 11 through 14, but it became much more highly translated following egg activation, increasing by 36 fold in the activated egg relative to the stage 14 oocyte (median TE change, 1.2 fold).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data.

claim: bicoid mRNA translation increased by 36 fold in the activated egg relative to the stage 14 oocyte.
source: In our analyses, translation of bicoid mRNA was undetectable or detected with very few reads in oocytes from stages 11 through 14, but it became much more highly translated following egg activation, increasing by 36 fold in the activated egg relative to the stage 14 oocyte (median TE change, 1.2 fold).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data.

claim: torso mRNA TE increased 13 fold during egg activation.
source: mRNAs for torso and Toll were somewhat better translated in stage 14 oocytes, but nonetheless their TEs increased 13 and 46 fold, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Toll mRNA TE increased 46 fold during egg activation.
source: mRNAs for torso and Toll were somewhat better translated in stage 14 oocytes, but nonetheless their TEs increased 13 and 46 fold, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Toll poly(A)-tail length increased 3.3 fold during egg activation.
source: During this time, the Toll poly(A)-tail length increased 3.3 fold (median tail length change, 1.1 fold), which corresponded well to the trend observed globally for tail-length and TE changes (Figure 4C), suggesting that its increased tail-length might fully account for its increased TE.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the absence of cytoplasmic polyadenylation, Toll underwent substantial translational upregulation during egg activation and remained one of the most efficiently translated mRNAs in the wispy-mutant laid egg, despite having a mean tail length of only 14 nt.
source: Indeed, our subsequent experiments with wispy-mutant animals showed that in the absence of cytoplasmic polyadenylation, Toll underwent substantial translational upregulation during egg activation and remained one of the most efficiently translated mRNAs in the wispy-mutant laid egg, despite having a mean tail length of only 14 nt.
evidence: This is supported by data from wispy-mutant experiments.

claim: The poly(A)-tail lengths of bicoid and torso increased by only 1.7 and 1.3 fold during egg activation, respectively.
source: The poly(A)-tail lengths of bicoid and torso increased by only 1.7 and 1.3 fold, respectively, putting them outside the global trend (Figure 4C), and the unimodal tail-length distributions showed again that our focus on the mean change did not miss a unique behavior of a subpopulation of transcripts (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: bicoid mRNA had an average tail length of 42 nt in stage 14 oocytes.
source: Because bicoid mRNA had an average tail length of 42 nt in stage 14 oocytes, which was similar to that of many well translated mRNAs at this stage, we conclude that there was likely a translational repressor acting on it in oocytes to prevent its translation prior to egg activation.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PAL-seq data.

claim: There was likely a translational repressor acting on bicoid mRNA in oocytes to prevent its translation prior to egg activation.
source: Because bicoid mRNA had an average tail length of 42 nt in stage 14 oocytes, which was similar to that of many well translated mRNAs at this stage, we conclude that there was likely a translational repressor acting on it in oocytes to prevent its translation prior to egg activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bicoid has a long tail but is not translated in oocytes.

claim: Wispy is the cytoplasmic poly(A)-polymerase responsible for poly(A)-tail lengthening at the end of oocyte maturation and continuing through egg activation.
source: Wispy is the cytoplasmic poly(A)-polymerase responsible for poly(A)-tail lengthening at the end of oocyte maturation and continuing through egg activation (Benoit et al., 2008; Cui et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benoit et al., 2008 and Cui et al., 2008.

claim: Most maternal transcripts bind to oligo(dT) with less affinity in wispy mutants.
source: Indeed, within this developmental window, most maternal transcripts bind to oligo(dT) with less affinity in wispy mutants, indicating that many poly(A) tails shorten in the absence of Wispy (Cui et al., 2013), but the degree to which tail-lengths shorten and the impact on TE had not been previously measured.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cui et al., 2013.

claim: Of the mRNAs from 3571 genes measured in stage 13 oocytes, 1801 had tails that were at least 50% shorter in wispy-mutant oocytes relative to wild-type.
source: Of the mRNAs from 3571 genes measured in stage 13 oocytes, 1801 had tails that were at least 50% shorter in wispy-mutant oocytes relative to wild-type, and for all but a few mRNAs the poly(A) tail was at least somewhat shorter in the absence of Wispy (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PAL-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In wispy-mutant laid eggs, 1219 of the 1836 measured mRNAs had poly(A) tails at least 50% shorter than those in wild-type 0–1 hr embryos.
source: In wispy-mutant laid eggs, 1219 of the 1836 measured mRNAs had poly(A) tails at least 50% shorter than those in the analogous wild-type sample (0–1 hr embryos), and again for all but a few mRNAs the poly(A) tail was shorter in the absence of Wispy (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PAL-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mRNAs with tails that were least affected by the absence of Wispy showed a remarkable enrichment for mRNAs of ribosomal proteins, both in oocytes and laid eggs (p<10–41 and p<10–44, respectively).
source: Examination of the mRNAs with tails that were least affected by the absence of Wispy revealed a remarkable enrichment for mRNAs of ribosomal proteins, both in oocytes and laid eggs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; p<10–41 and p<10–44, respectively, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The global changes in poly(A)-tail length that occurred in the absence of Wispy did not affect the coupling between poly(A)-tail length and TE.
source: Strikingly, the global changes in poly(A)-tail length that occurred in the absence of Wispy did not affect the coupling between poly(A)-tail length and TE.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In wispy-mutant stage 13 oocytes and laid eggs, poly(A)-tail length and TE were correlated to a similar extent as in wild-type oocytes and embryos.
source: In wispy-mutant stage 13 oocytes and laid eggs, poly(A)-tail length and TE were correlated to a similar extent as in wild-type oocytes and embryos (Figure 1B, 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 1B, 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The strong correlation between changes in poly(A)-tail length and changes in TE that occurred at egg activation in wild-type flies was retained in wispy-mutant flies.
source: Importantly, the strong correlation between changes in poly(A)-tail length and changes in TE that occurred at egg activation in wild-type flies was retained in wispy-mutant flies (Figures 1B and 5C, respectively), indicating that changes in the length of the poly(A) tail—not the act of cytoplasmic polyadenylation per se—is what influences TE.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 1B and 5C.

claim: Changes in the length of the poly(A) tail—not the act of cytoplasmic polyadenylation per se—is what influences TE.
source: Importantly, the strong correlation between changes in poly(A)-tail length and changes in TE that occurred at egg activation in wild-type flies was retained in wispy-mutant flies (Figures 1B and 5C, respectively), indicating that changes in the length of the poly(A) tail—not the act of cytoplasmic polyadenylation per se—is what influences TE.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TE-tail length coupling is preserved in wispy mutants.

claim: The changes in TE that occurred during egg activation in wispy-mutant samples strongly correlated with those in the wild-type samples.
source: Moreover, the changes in TE that occurred during egg activation in wispy-mutant samples strongly correlated with those in the wild-type samples, as did the relative changes in poly(A)-tail length (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The relative changes in poly(A)-tail length during egg activation in wispy-mutant samples strongly correlated with those in wild-type samples.
source: Moreover, the changes in TE that occurred during egg activation in wispy-mutant samples strongly correlated with those in the wild-type samples, as did the relative changes in poly(A)-tail length (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cytoplasmic polyadenylation was largely dispensable for reshaping TEs during egg activation, as the rank order of tail-length and TE changes at this time were largely preserved in the wispy-mutant samples.
source: Thus, although Wispy lengthens the poly(A)-tails of most mRNAs during egg activation, our results indicated that this lengthening was largely dispensable for reshaping TEs during egg activation, as the rank order of tail-length and TE changes at this time were largely preserved in the wispy-mutant samples.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation of changes between wild-type and wispy-mutant samples.

claim: The RPFs in wild-type and wispy-mutant stage 13 oocytes were well correlated (Rs = 0.76).
source: The RPFs in wild-type and wispy-mutant stage 13 oocytes were well correlated, and the same was true for 0–1 hr wild-type embryos compared with wispy-mutant laid eggs (Rs = 0.76 for both, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The RPFs in 0–1 hr wild-type embryos and wispy-mutant laid eggs were well correlated (Rs = 0.76).
source: The RPFs in wild-type and wispy-mutant stage 13 oocytes were well correlated, and the same was true for 0–1 hr wild-type embryos compared with wispy-mutant laid eggs (Rs = 0.76 for both, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: cortex is a known target of Wispy, the upregulation of which is essential for the OET.
source: Included among these was cortex, a known target of Wispy, the upregulation of which is essential for the OET (Chu et al., 2001; Benoit et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chu et al., 2001 and Benoit et al., 2008.

claim: During egg activation in Drosophila, cytoplasmic polyadenylation extends the tails of nearly all mRNAs but does not play the major role in generating the relative differences in tail lengths and TEs observed between mRNAs.
source: We conclude that during egg activation in Drosophila, cytoplasmic polyadenylation extends the tails of nearly all mRNAs but does not play the major role in generating the relative differences in tail lengths and TEs observed between mRNAs, which implies that poly(A)-tail shortening instead plays the major role in generating these differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the wispy-mutant experiments showing preserved rank order of changes.

claim: Poly(A)-tail shortening plays the major role in generating the relative differences in tail lengths and TEs observed between mRNAs during egg activation.
source: We conclude that during egg activation in Drosophila, cytoplasmic polyadenylation extends the tails of nearly all mRNAs but does not play the major role in generating the relative differences in tail lengths and TEs observed between mRNAs, which implies that poly(A)-tail shortening instead plays the major role in generating these differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the wispy-mutant experiments.

claim: The PNG kinase is required for nuclear divisions in the early embryo.
source: The PNG kinase, which is required for nuclear divisions in the early embryo, influences the translational up- or downregulation of hundreds of different mRNAs at egg activation (Figure 6A) (Kronja et al., 2014b), presumably through its regulation of translational regulators, such as SMG (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PNG influences the translational up- or downregulation of hundreds of different mRNAs at egg activation.
source: The PNG kinase, which is required for nuclear divisions in the early embryo, influences the translational up- or downregulation of hundreds of different mRNAs at egg activation (Figure 6A) (Kronja et al., 2014b), presumably through its regulation of translational regulators, such as SMG (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and citation to Kronja et al., 2014b.

claim: PNG presumably regulates translational regulators, such as SMG.
source: The PNG kinase, which is required for nuclear divisions in the early embryo, influences the translational up- or downregulation of hundreds of different mRNAs at egg activation (Figure 6A) (Kronja et al., 2014b), presumably through its regulation of translational regulators, such as SMG (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros et al., 2007 and is speculative.

claim: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were highly correlated between png-mutant and wild-type stage 14 oocytes.
source: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were highly correlated between png-mutant and wild-type stage 14 oocytes, whereas the correlation was substantially lower between png-mutant and wild-type activated eggs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The correlation between poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs was substantially lower between png-mutant and wild-type activated eggs compared to stage 14 oocytes.
source: Poly(A)-tail lengths and TEs were highly correlated between png-mutant and wild-type stage 14 oocytes, whereas the correlation was substantially lower between png-mutant and wild-type activated eggs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The requirement of PNG for achieving the gene-expression profile of the wild-type activated egg but not the stage 14 oocyte was consistent with PNG kinase becoming active during egg activation to serve as a master regulator of the OET.
source: The requirement of PNG for achieving the gene-expression profile of the wild-type activated egg but not the stage 14 oocyte was consistent with PNG kinase becoming active during egg activation to serve as a master regulator of the OET (Shamanski and Orr-Weaver, 1991; Kronja et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations.

claim: The set of mRNAs dependent on PNG for their translational downregulation was predominantly those that underwent tail-length shortening during egg activation in wild-type samples.
source: The set of mRNAs dependent on PNG for their translational downregulation was predominantly those that underwent tail-length shortening during egg activation in wild-type samples (median TE log2 fold change of –3.03 after median centering and median tail-length log2 fold change of –0.35) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In png-mutant embryos, mRNAs dependent on PNG for translational downregulation failed to be deadenylated.
source: In png-mutant embryos, these mRNAs failed to be deadenylated, as expected if tail-length shortening mediated their translational repression (median TE log2 fold change of 0.10 after median centering and median tail-length log2 fold change of 0.32, which closely resembled the median value for all mRNAs) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The set of mRNAs dependent on PNG for their translational upregulation was predominantly those that underwent tail-length extension during wild-type egg activation.
source: Correspondingly, the set of mRNAs dependent on PNG for their translational upregulation was predominantly those that underwent tail-length extension during wild-type egg activation (median TE log2 fold change of 2.98 after median centering and median tail-length log2 fold change of 0.62), and these mRNAs failed to undergo tail lengthening in png mutants, again as expected if tail-lengthening mediated their translational activation (median TE log2 fold change of 0.36 after median centering and median tail-length log2 fold change of 0.32, which closely resembled the median value for all mRNAs) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PNG plays a central role in regulating polyadenylation and deadenylation for the hundreds of mRNAs present at egg activation.
source: mRNAs that were translationally up- or downregulated by PNG also typically increased or decreased in poly(A)-tail length, respectively (Figure 6D), and the tail-length changes for either the up- or downregulated sets of mRNAs were largely dependent on PNG (Figure 6B and C), which showed that PNG plays a central role in regulating polyadenylation and deadenylation for the hundreds of mRNAs present at egg activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: SMG is reported to downregulate translation of its target mRNAs through either direct recruitment of the deadenylation machinery or recruitment of CUP.
source: SMG is reported to downregulate translation of its target mRNAs through either direct recruitment of the deadenylation machinery or recruitment of CUP, which directly represses translation initiation and can also promote deadenylation (Nelson et al., 2004; Semotok et al., 2005; Igreja and Izaurralde, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2004; Semotok et al., 2005; Igreja and Izaurralde, 2011.

claim: In the absence of SMG, the poly(A)-tail lengths for the set of PNG-dependent downregulated mRNAs were less shortened during egg activation.
source: Our results showed that in the absence of SMG, the poly(A)-tail lengths for the set of PNG-dependent downregulated mRNAs were less shortened during egg activation (median tail-length log2 fold changes of –0.22 and –0.04 for the wild-type and smg mutant, respectively, relative to the median of all mRNAs, p<10–27, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test), and this coincided with their partial translational derepression (median TE log2 fold change of –2.2 and –1.2, respectively, after median centering, p<10–32, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the absence of SMG, PNG-dependent downregulated mRNAs showed partial translational derepression.
source: Our results showed that in the absence of SMG, the poly(A)-tail lengths for the set of PNG-dependent downregulated mRNAs were less shortened during egg activation (median tail-length log2 fold changes of –0.22 and –0.04 for the wild-type and smg mutant, respectively, relative to the median of all mRNAs, p<10–27, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test), and this coincided with their partial translational derepression (median TE log2 fold change of –2.2 and –1.2, respectively, after median centering, p<10–32, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No significant difference was observed for either poly(A)-tail length or TE changes for the PNG-dependent upregulated mRNAs in smg mutants.
source: In contrast, no significant difference was observed for either poly(A)-tail length or TE changes for the PNG-dependent upregulated mRNAs (median tail-length log2 fold changes of 0.27 for both the wild-type and smg mutant relative to the median of all mRNAs, and median TE log2 fold changes of 2.8 and 2.7, respectively, after median centering for the wild-type and smg mutant, p=0.89 and 0.37 for tail-length or TE changes, respectively, two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test), consistent with SMG functioning only as a repressor (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SMG functions only as a repressor.
source: In contrast, no significant difference was observed for either poly(A)-tail length or TE changes for the PNG-dependent upregulated mRNAs (median tail-length log2 fold changes of 0.27 for both the wild-type and smg mutant relative to the median of all mRNAs, and median TE log2 fold changes of 2.8 and 2.7, respectively, after median centering for the wild-type and smg mutant, p=0.89 and 0.37 for tail-length or TE changes, respectively, two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test), consistent with SMG functioning only as a repressor (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SMG affects only downregulated mRNAs.

claim: Recruitment of deadenylases was the dominant mechanism of SMG-dependent translational repression occurring during egg activation and early embryogenesis.
source: In general, mRNAs that were translationally repressed by SMG also decreased in poly-(A)-tail length, which indicated that recruitment of deadenylases was the dominant mechanism of SMG-dependent translational repression occurring during egg activation and early embryogenesis (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between SMG-dependent TE changes and tail-length changes shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the absence of SMG, a set of mRNAs reported to be bound by SMG in the early embryo had longer poly(A) tails and were better translated following the OET.
source: Additionally, in the absence of SMG, a set of mRNAs reported to be bound by SMG in the early embryo (Chen et al., 2014) had longer poly(A) tails and were better translated following the OET (median tail-length log2 fold changes of –0.21 and –0.04 for the wild-type and smg mutant, respectively, relative to the median of all mRNAs, and median TE log2 fold changes of –1.0 and –0.15, respectively, after median centering, p<10–16 and 10–11 for tail length or TE changes, respectively, one-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: SMG mediates much of the PNG-dependent translational repression occurring during egg activation and early embryogenesis, with most of this repression attributable to poly(A)-tail shortening.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that SMG mediates much of the PNG-dependent translational repression occurring during egg activation and early embryogenesis, with most of this repression attributable to poly(A)-tail shortening.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The residual repression observed in the absence of SMG indicates that one or more additional PNG-activated translational repressors also operate during egg activation and early embryogenesis.
source: Nevertheless, the residual repression observed in the absence of SMG (Figure 7A) indicates that one or more additional PNG-activated translational repressors also operate at this time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some repression remains in smg mutants.

claim: The developmental shift in the nature of translational control observed in vertebrates also occurs in flies.
source: These results showed that the developmental shift in the nature of translational control observed in vertebrates also occurs in flies; in Drosophila, just as in zebrafish and Xenopus (Subtelny et al., 2014), the coupling between poly(A)-tail length and TE observed in the early embryo disappeared around gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and citation to Subtelny et al., 2014.

claim: In Drosophila, the coupling between poly(A)-tail length and TE observed in the early embryo disappeared around gastrulation.
source: These results showed that the developmental shift in the nature of translational control observed in vertebrates also occurs in flies; in Drosophila, just as in zebrafish and Xenopus (Subtelny et al., 2014), the coupling between poly(A)-tail length and TE observed in the early embryo disappeared around gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The uncoupling of TE from poly(A)-tail length is a broadly conserved developmental switch in the nature of translational control, occurring around the onset of gastrulation in both vertebrate and invertebrate embryos.
source: The uncoupling of TE from poly(A)-tail length is thus a broadly conserved developmental switch in the nature of translational control, occurring around the onset of gastrulation in both vertebrate and invertebrate embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in Drosophila, zebrafish, and Xenopus.

claim: PABP is limiting in the developmental stages in which tail length and TE are coupled, such that mRNAs are competing for PABP.
source: However, repeating our analyses using absolute tail-length changes rather than tail-length log2 fold changes yielded the same results for the respective comparisons, with nearly identical Rs values (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggesting that PABP is limiting in the developmental stages in which tail length and TE are coupled, such that mRNAs are competing for PABP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that relative and absolute tail-length changes give similar correlations.

claim: The correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE reflects a causal relationship, i.e., that changes in poly(A)-tail length at least partially cause the corresponding changes in TE.
source: We presume that the correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE that we observed in oocytes and pre-gastrulation embryos reflects a causal relationship, i.e., that changes in poly(A)-tail length at least partially cause the corresponding changes in TE.
evidence: This is inferred from previous single-gene studies and the current observations.

claim: Previous single-gene studies clearly demonstrate a causal role for cytoplasmic polyadenylation, and poly(A)-tail length itself, in regulating the translation of mRNAs during oocyte maturation and early embryogenesis.
source: Because previous single-gene studies clearly demonstrate a causal role for cytoplasmic polyadenylation, and poly(A)-tail length itself, in regulating the translation of mRNAs during these developmental times (McGrew et al., 1989; Salles et al., 1994; Barkoff et al., 1998), we interpret our observation of a global correlation between poly(A)-tail length and TE as reflecting a causal relationship between the two wherein tail-length changes cause TE changes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to McGrew et al., 1989; Salles et al., 1994; Barkoff et al., 1998.

claim: Widespread changes in poly(A)-tail length broadly reshape the translational profiles of oocytes and early embryos.
source: Given this interpretation, our results indicate that widespread changes in poly(A)-tail length broadly reshape the translational profiles of oocytes and early embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the causal relationship between tail-length and TE changes.

claim: Tail-length–independent processes often act concordantly with tail-length–dependent processes and thereby amplify the apparent effects of tail-length changes.
source: Indeed, we suspect that tail-length–independent processes often act concordantly with tail-length–dependent processes and thereby amplify the apparent effects of tail-length changes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain observations of disproportionate TE changes.

claim: In Drosophila, the first 13 division cycles occur in a nuclear syncytium.
source: In Drosophila, the first 13 division cycles occur in a nuclear syncytium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Cellularization (at 2–3 hr of embryogenesis) marks completion of the MZT and is immediately followed by the morphogenetic movements of gastrulation.
source: Cellularization (at 2–3 hr of embryogenesis) marks completion of the MZT and is immediately followed by the morphogenetic movements of gastrulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Early embryogenesis is controlled by maternal mRNAs.
source: Thus, early embryogenesis is controlled by maternal mRNAs, and based on the studies of mRNAs from a few genes (Salles et al., 1994; Lieberfarb et al., 1996), those with longer poly(A)-tails would be predicted to have higher TEs, as observed in vertebrate systems (Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stage 11 oocytes are arrested in prophase I.
source: Stage 11 oocytes are arrested in prophase I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: Nuclear envelope breakdown occurs between stages 12 and 13.
source: Nuclear envelope breakdown, a hallmark of the release of this arrest, occurs between stages 12 and 13 (Von Stetina et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2009), and the oocytes arrest in metaphase I during stage 14, the final stage of oogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Von Stetina et al., 2008 and Hughes et al., 2009.

claim: Oocytes arrest in metaphase I during stage 14, the final stage of oogenesis.
source: Nuclear envelope breakdown, a hallmark of the release of this arrest, occurs between stages 12 and 13 (Von Stetina et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2009), and the oocytes arrest in metaphase I during stage 14, the final stage of oogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: wispy-mutant eggs do not complete meiosis and thus do not begin nuclear divisions.
source: Although wispy-mutant eggs do not complete meiosis and thus do not begin nuclear divisions, most of the molecular changes characteristic of the OET are independent of these divisions, motivating a comparison of wispy-mutant laid eggs with wild-type early embryos.
evidence: This is established knowledge about wispy mutants.

claim: Most of the molecular changes characteristic of the OET are independent of nuclear divisions.
source: Although wispy-mutant eggs do not complete meiosis and thus do not begin nuclear divisions, most of the molecular changes characteristic of the OET are independent of these divisions, motivating a comparison of wispy-mutant laid eggs with wild-type early embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability to compare wispy-mutant laid eggs with wild-type embryos.

claim: smg mRNA is translationally repressed in the mature oocyte by PUM.
source: smg mRNA is translationally repressed in the mature oocyte by PUM, and at egg activation this repression is relieved by the PAN GU (PNG) protein kinase complex (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros et al., 2007.

claim: At egg activation, repression of smg mRNA is relieved by the PAN GU (PNG) protein kinase complex.
source: smg mRNA is translationally repressed in the mature oocyte by PUM, and at egg activation this repression is relieved by the PAN GU (PNG) protein kinase complex (Tadros et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadros et al., 2007.
